Mockus, Rigby, Nagappan), 'Automating Low-Risk Code Review at Meta: RADAR, Risk Calibration, and Review Efficiency', arXiv:2605.30208v2, 12 Jun 2026, https://arxiv.org/html/2605.30208 ; (4) Rahman, Alam, Roy, Roy, 'Who Pays the Review Cost? Triage, Fairness, and Accountability in AI-authored Pull Requests', arXiv:2610.11179, 8 Oct 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11179 ; (5) Robert Kimani, 'Your engineering strategy has a new failure mode', LeadDev, 12 Oct 2026, https://leaddev.com/leadership/your-engineering-strategy-has-a-new-failure-mode ; (6) CloudBees press release 19 May 2026 and 2026 State of Code Abundance blog; (7) Keith Williams, Cal.com blog on PR review, 11 May 2026, https://cal.com/blog/dedicated-pr-review-rotation ; (8) Fred Hebert, Honeycomb, 'Embracing the code review bottleneck', 22 Jul 2026.
source_tier: Mixed: Meta RADAR is a company-authored paper published at PACMSE (ASE track; peer-review status of the venue not independently checked) [uncertain]; Rahman et al. is a preprint with a survey; Pragmatic Engineer, Cal.com, Honeycomb are practitioner posts; LeadDev is a practitioner opinion piece; CloudBees is vendor research.
access_status: Opened by fetch: Pragmatic Engineer 8 Sep piece (partly paywalled, sections 1-3 read, section 4 'Produce less code' not read); Pragmatic Engineer Pulse piece (free, read, but gave no detail on capacity/ownership); Meta RADAR HTML (read via summarising fetch, some figures garbled); Rahman et al. abstract page (read, paraphrase only; PDF body not readable, so method detail beyond abstract not verified); LeadDev Kimani article (read via summarising fetch); CloudBees press release and State of Code Abundance blog (read); Cal.com (read); Honeycomb (read). CloudBees 57% vs 35% figure: NOT FOUND in either CloudBees page; the full CloudBees report PDF was not opened. Not opened: Cloudflare, Faire, HubSpot, Uber primary engineering posts; Anthropic/OpenAI claims are Orosz's secondhand report. All fetches were through a summarising tool, so quotes are as returned by it, not checked against raw page text [uncertain].
sponsor_and_incentive: CloudBees sells CI/CD and 'governance' tooling and commissioned TrendCandy for the survey. Meta authors are Meta employees describing Meta's own system. Pragmatic Engineer is an independent newsletter (paid tier). Cal.com and Honeycomb are product companies writing about their own practice. Kimani is a freelance Linux engineer/consultant. Rahman et al. are academic (no sponsor seen in abstract). Semgrep, CodeRabbit and other vendor blogs surfaced in search were not used as evidence.
exact_quotes: Pragmatic Engineer 8 Sep 2026 (via fetch, sections 1-3): at Anthropic 'a human merges even low-risk changes', goal eventually 'another Claude instance merge low-risk changes'.
Pragmatic Engineer 8 Sep 2026: Duckbill Group moved to risk-based review; changes to 'the public API/MCP, auth, design system' needed human review, enforced by a shell script adding a GitHub label.
Pragmatic Engineer 8 Sep 2026: Weaviate CTO Etienne Dilocker: '90% is left to agents, with humans in the loop for critical scope decisions.'
Meta RADAR (arXiv:2605.30208): ACE 'is intended to allow changes from automated sources to land without any human review.'
Meta RADAR: 'Diffs that pass receive RADAR Approval, meaning no human review is required'; also 'a human reviewer can still reject the diff.'
Meta RADAR limitation: 'because diffs are not randomly assigned to RADAR, unobserved confounding can influence observed changes.'
Kimani, LeadDev: '57% identified reviewing, testing, and deploying code as the delivery bottleneck.' (Kimani attributes this to a CloudBees survey.)
Kimani, LeadDev: 'Reassess if review capacity grows slower than implementation' (assumption-table trigger, review time as signal).
Kimani, LeadDev: 'The leader responsible for a strategic bet should own its decision threshold.'
CloudBees State of Code Abundance blog: 'writing code is no longer the primary bottleneck. Governing it is.'
CloudBees press release: '70% now view test suite maintenance as a bigger burden than writing code itself.'
Cal.com: 'If you have 5 PRs open, draft and non-draft combined, do not start something new.'
Cal.com: a 'focused ~1,000-line PR that solves one clear problem is fine'; well past 1,000 lines is 'a strong signal to split.'
Honeycomb (Hebert): 'we need to review the plan and prompt given to the AI that is writing the code.'
key_claims: Pragmatic Engineer (8 Sep 2026): CTOs are responding to review overload with blast-radius or risk-based routing. Anthropic and OpenAI (per Orosz's conversations) keep a human merge even for low-risk changes. Duckbill Group (about 15 people) dropped human review for low-risk PRs and kept it for public API/MCP, auth and design system. Uber's Code Inbox flags high-impact changes. Review rotas not mentioned in the visible text.

Pragmatic Engineer Pulse (Jul 2026): Cloudflare, Faire and HubSpot each built in-house AI review tools; the visible text says nothing about who owns review capacity. Uber Code Inbox has 'smart assignments' and 'Risk Profiles'.

Meta RADAR: a layered funnel (eligibility checks, heuristics, ML Diff Risk Score, LLM review agent, deterministic validation) routes low-risk diffs to automated approval and everything else to human review. Motivation is code volume growth outpacing human review. Accountability stays with authors, with a delayed landing window in which a human can reject.

Rahman et al. (survey of 239 practitioners from 31 countries): AI authorship alone did not make reviewers reject a PR. Willingness to review depended on accountability: bounded scope, project-grounded rationale, validation beyond CI, contributor responsiveness, and clear ownership after merge. Missing these is 'reviewability debt'. Respondents report routing and deferral when human oversight is hard to see.

Kimani (LeadDev): strategy goes stale as AI shifts delivery constraints. Treats review capacity as a leading signal to monitor and says leaders should own decision thresholds. Does not discuss code review ownership in depth.
CloudBees: writing code is no longer the primary bottleneck, governing it is. The specific 57%/35% comparison is cited by Kimani but I could not find it on CloudBees pages.

Cal.com: individual authors cap open PRs at five and split PRs past about 1,000 lines. This is a norm in a blog post, not shown as tooling enforcement. No review rota or turnaround target described in the body, despite the URL slug.
Honeycomb: reviews the plan and prompt, not just code; reviewer involvement scales with complexity; reports velocity held. No rota or size cap.
headline_figures: Duckbill Group (Pragmatic Engineer, 8 Sep 2026): merged PRs rose from 353 to 684 after dropping review for low-risk PRs; median merge time 26h for human-reviewed vs 1h without; 60 open PRs on a team of five before the change. Period and exact comparison window not visible in the fetched text [uncertain]. Single small team, self-reported.
Pragmatic Engineer: GitHub PRs opened up fivefold over three years; PRs and commits nearly doubled from end of 2025. Secondhand GitHub data, not verified at source [uncertain].

Meta RADAR: 535,290 RADAR-reviewed diffs, 331,720 landed; median review wall time 35% lower than human-reviewed diffs; lines per landed diff up 105.9% and diffs per developer up 51% year on year, over 80% of increase attributed to agentic AI. Paper also states a 'over 330%' reduction in time to close, which is not a coherent percentage reduction, so treat with caution. Revert and incident rates reported as fractions of non-RADAR rates (garbled in fetch, possibly 1/3 and 1/50) [uncertain]. Share of diffs reviewed within 24h is said to be falling, no number given.
Rahman et al.: n=239 practitioners, 31 countries, self-reported plus scenario questions.

CloudBees: 213 enterprise technology leaders (release says 'more than 200'), survey by TrendCandy, May 19 2026, margin of error +/-8% at 95%. 70% say test suite maintenance is a bigger burden than writing code; 81% report production failures tied to AI-generated code. The user's lead figure (57% name review, testing and deployment as the bottleneck vs 35% for writing code) was NOT confirmed on CloudBees pages. Only the 57% appears, in Kimani's LeadDev article, attributed to CloudBees; the 35% figure was not found anywhere I opened [uncertain]. A search summary attributed 57% (manual human review of every line of AI code) to a Harness study, a different claim; not opened.
Cal.com: cap of 5 open PRs per author; about 1,000 lines as the point to split. No turnaround numbers.
sample_and_method: Meta: production telemetry from Meta's monorepo, observational before/after on threshold change (P25 to P50) and difference-in-differences for efficiency. Rahman et al.: online survey of 239 practitioners in 31 countries, scenario-based plus self-report. CloudBees: survey of 213 leaders by TrendCandy. Pragmatic Engineer: Orosz's interviews with CTOs and founders, anecdotal, small named companies. Cal.com, Honeycomb, Kimani: single-author practitioner accounts, no measurement beyond self-report.
limitations: Meta: one company's monorepo, no random assignment, parallel-trend assumptions not fully specified, reverts are imperfect proxies for harm, data not released; the 'over 330%' claim is incoherent. Meta's setting (mature tooling, ML risk model) is not transferable to a typical team. Duckbill is a five-person-scale team and self-reported. Pragmatic Engineer routing details are secondhand and partly paywalled; I did not see its section on PR size limits. Rahman et al. captures stated willingness, not behaviour, and I only read the abstract. No source I opened measures who is formally accountable for review capacity or tests a review rota; Cal.com and Honeycomb give no rota detail. No source opened shows a size cap enforced in tooling (Cal.com's is a written norm). CloudBees 57%/35% unverified at source. All pages read through a summarising fetch tool, so wording may be imperfect.
what_a_leader_can_do: Supported actions: (1) route by what a change touches, with named high-risk paths needing human review enforced by labels or checks (Duckbill, Uber Risk Profiles, Meta RADAR). Evidence: moderate at Meta (large observational data, one company), weak elsewhere (anecdote). (2) Track review capacity against implementation volume as an explicit leading signal and owner-assigned trigger (Kimani; opinion, weak evidence). (3) Require accountability evidence on incoming PRs: bounded scope, rationale, validation beyond CI, named post-merge owner (Rahman et al.; survey of stated willingness, moderate). (4) Cap open PRs per author and split large PRs (Cal.com; practitioner norm, no outcome data). Not supported by anything opened: that a rota fixes capacity, or that a leader-level owner of review capacity improves outcomes. That gap is itself worth stating in the essay.
overlap_with_site_essays: High with Checking Isn't Catching and What It Takes to Trust Agent Output (risk-based routing, human-in-loop limits, Meta finding that automated review caught issues humans would not). Moderate with The Verification Gap (CloudBees governance framing, Kimani). Low with Overseeing Agents Is the Tiring Part, except Rahman et al. 'scarce reviewer attention' and 'reviewability debt'.
